item.title: Beyond the cloud: Why businesses are turning to on-device AI
item.description:
At TechSparks 2026, Brilyant CEO Akash Saxenaa explained how running AI models locally can help businesses control costs, protect sensitive data, and reduce their dependence on the cloud.

item.content:encoded:
AI tools have made it easier for businesses to analyze documents, generate content, and automate tasks. But how much do companies know about where the data they enter into these tools goes?

At TechSparks 2026, Akash Saxenaa, CEO of Brilyant, discussed why businesses should consider moving routine AI workloads from the cloud to local devices. He argued that on-device AI can help organizations manage costs, protect data, and reduce their dependence on internet connectivity.

The costs of taking AI to the cloud

The economics of AI are changing. While the cost of individual tokens may be falling, Saxenaa pointed out that inference costs could rise as businesses deploy more AI agents and consume more tokens. Citing Gartner, he referred to predictions that inference costs could increase more than fivefold.

Cost is only one concern. When employees use cloud-based AI tools, sensitive business information may leave the organization’s own environment. This raises questions about data privacy, intellectual property protection, and compliance with data protection requirements.

Saxenaa cited India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act as another reason for businesses to review their AI infrastructure.

“If you look at 83% of Indian enterprises, they have not yet begun comprehensive DPDP implementations, or they are not even aware. What is the cost? Rs 250 crore. Now, if you are a large company, 5,000 employees, that’s a budget line. But if you are an SMB, that's a company,” he said.

For smaller businesses, in particular, the financial consequences of non-compliance could be significant.

Saxenaa’s recommendation is to bring the model to the data rather than take the data to the model.

Not every task requires a frontier model

Saxenaa compared cloud-based AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude with on-device AI, where models run locally.

Cloud-based tools can involve recurring input and output token costs, latency, and less direct control over where data is processed. On-device AI, by contrast, can operate without an internet connection and does not incur recurring token charges for local inference.

“Almost 60-70% of your workload can move on to on-device. But the balance 30%, you will have to use large, complex, latest front-end AI models," Saxenaa said.

He stressed that the two approaches are not mutually exclusive. Businesses can use larger cloud-based models for complex tasks while moving suitable everyday workloads to local devices.

On-device AI: From the office to the factory floor

Saxenaa outlined several areas where businesses could use on-device AI, including endpoint security, support operations, internal search, and finance.

“There are these beautiful use cases out there for on-device: you look at endpoint security or support operations. All those things can be done on-device. You look at finance, local rack, internal search, finance, operations. Everything can be done on-device,” he said.

For software development teams, keeping code on local devices can reduce the risk of intellectual property being exposed through cloud-based tools.

In contact centers, on-device AI can support real-time call translation, note-taking, and product recommendations. These functions can operate locally, reducing dependence on network connectivity.

Saxenaa also highlighted devices equipped with neural processing units (NPUs), which allow AI models to run locally. This can help reduce recurring cloud costs while supporting data governance and operational resilience.

During his keynote, Saxenaa presented a case study involving Tech Paramount Solutions to show how on-device AI could be used in an industrial setting.

The company’s TP Smart Sol platform combines visitor and vehicle management, asset management, energy monitoring, surveillance, and workforce management.

With Brilyant's support, Tech Paramount Solutions explored using Apple's Mac mini as an edge-computing device to process video analytics locally, while keeping its platform connected to the cloud for alerts, dashboards, and remote access.

The setup can process live AI video analytics from around 100 on-premise cameras.

Tech Paramount Solutions' co-founder shared that deployment reduced annual security overhead by more than Rs 12 lakh, cut lifetime compute costs by over Rs 11 lakh per Mac mini compared with comparable GPU-based options, and increased factory machine uptime by more than 240 hours a month.

Making on-device AI work at scale

Moving AI workloads to local devices involves more than installing a model. Businesses also need to consider device management, security, governance, and the infrastructure required to support large-scale deployments.

Saxenaa explained how Brilyant works with partners including Apple and Jamf to provide device provisioning, AI setup, and lifecycle management. Leasing and financing options can help businesses spread the upfront cost of devices over time.

For organizations managing hundreds of laptops, Brilyant also offers containerized runtimes and governance measures designed to keep data within controlled environments.

The larger challenge is deciding which AI workloads should run locally, which require cloud-based models, and how to manage data and devices across an organization.

On-device AI will not eliminate the need for the cloud. However, as more capable models become available for local hardware, businesses have more options to balance cost, privacy, and performance.

For Saxenaa, the shift is not about using AI everywhere in the same way, but deciding where workloads should run and where business data should remain.

item.title: Why storytelling can be a startup's strongest competitive moat
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, explained why founders need to tell authentic, distinctive stories and how storytelling can help build trust and differentiate a business.
item.content:encoded:
Technology, capital, and talent can help startups build and scale their businesses. But as competitors gain access to similar resources, founders also need to explain what makes their companies different.

At TechSparks 2026, Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, spoke about the role of storytelling in building a business.

Leading a masterclass titled ‘Startups and Storytelling: Making Narrative Your Moat’, Kohli said founders often treat storytelling as something to consider after developing their products. However, before achieving product-market fit, their story is often what they are selling.

“Every startup is a story no one believes in yet,” she said.

The ‘why’ behind the business

Kohli began by asking the audience why storytelling matters. Participants spoke about building trust, creating personal connections, and differentiating a business.

She then used her own career to demonstrate what founders often leave out of their stories.

After summarizing nearly 28 years of work in a few minutes, she asked the audience what was missing. It was the reason behind her decision to establish Startup Policy Forum.

While she had explained how founders approached her to work with them, she had not mentioned the gap she had identified: India lacked an institution to represent the startup ecosystem’s policy concerns to the government.

Kohli said a mission alone does not make a startup distinctive because competitors may have similar goals.

Founders must also explain why them—what makes them suited to building the business—and why now—what makes the timing relevant.

Their passion and the community supporting their work also help make the story harder to replicate, she said.

Why details matter

Kohli said people tend to remember stories more easily than statistics. Instead of simply presenting market-size figures, founders should explain how their products could change someone's life.

She encouraged them to use techniques learned in school English classes, including anecdotes, sensory details, drama and emotion.

Drawing on her own experiences, Kohli described how Startup Policy Forum's logo came about.

An early backer had dismissed her initial designs as “tacky”. The eventual idea came to her while watching her son play with a Rubik's Cube.

She also recalled how a chance meeting with a member at an airport became a social media post that gained traction. On another occasion, a session she attended at an awards evening reminded her of how the forum got its name and prompted a LinkedIn post.

Her point was that founders need not wait for major milestones to find stories worth sharing.

She advised them to document the early stages of their businesses, from the first garage office and notebooks to whiteboards and the arrival of their first employee.

For founders who struggle to write, Kohli suggested talking through their experiences with a friend, recording the conversation using an AI voice tool and turning the transcript into a post.

“You'll realize that you've actually said it well,” she said.

Using AI without losing authenticity

Kohli said AI has made storytelling easier, but it has also made it harder to stand out.

Generic stories can now be produced in seconds, and readers can often recognize content that does not reflect a founder's own experience.

She encouraged founders to use AI to improve their language, but not to generate facts or experiences.

“You can write stories; you can't cook them,” she said.

Referring to her own experience with the Rubik's Cube, Kohli said AI could help present the incident more clearly, but should not add details that never happened.

She also stressed the importance of consistency. Founders may speak to investors, customers, the media, and government representatives, but the underlying story should remain the same. Changing it to suit different audiences can affect credibility.

Knowing when to tell the story

The masterclass also addressed how often founders should communicate and when their public presence could become a distraction.

Kohli said storytelling should accompany meaningful business developments, such as a new feature, product launch, or milestone.

However, founders must balance the time spent communicating with the time needed to build their businesses.

She also cautioned that a founder’s public presence could become a liability if not managed carefully.

While formats and audiences may change, Kohli said the facts behind a founder’s story must remain consistent.

Storytelling can help startups attract attention, build trust, and connect with their audiences. But those stories need to be based on real experiences rather than manufactured narratives.

Edited by Teja Lele

item.title: 5 lessons from Hospitality with a Heart by Amrita Tripathi
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Hospitality with a Heart by Amrita Tripathi, a book exploring identity, acceptance, empathy and workplace inclusion.
item.content:encoded:
The stories that deserve to be heard are not always the ones that get told. Some remain hidden behind societal expectations, fear of judgement and the struggle to find acceptance.

I recently attended the launch of Hospitality with a Heart, written by Amrita Tripathi, with an introduction by Keshav Suri, Executive Director of The LaLiT Suri Hospitality Group. Held on October 31, 2026, at the Crystal Ballroom of The LaLiT New Delhi, the event brought together the people behind the book and those who have been part of the organisation's inclusion journey.

The book documents the personal journeys and lived experiences of queer team members at The LaLiT, exploring themes of identity, discrimination, resilience, acceptance and belonging.

The evening began with a welcome address by Dr Jyotsna Suri, Chairperson and Managing Director of The LaLiT Suri Hospitality Group, followed by a keynote address by Saurabh Kirpal. A panel discussion moderated by journalist Faye D'Souza, featuring Amrita Tripathi, Rithik Hukku, Shaurya and Shruti, explored workplace inclusion, queer representation and the importance of empathy.

The launch also featured the unveiling of the book by the Group's leadership and the people whose stories it captures, followed by drag performances by Hash Brownie and Hiten Noonwal.

Beyond the celebrations, what stood out was the larger message of creating spaces where people are not merely included but genuinely accepted.

5 Important lessons readers can take away from Hospitality with a Heart

1. True inclusion begins with acceptance

One of the central ideas explored in Hospitality with a Heart is that inclusion goes beyond simply allowing people to be part of an organisation.

For individuals from marginalised communities, finding acceptance can be a difficult journey. Social expectations, discrimination, bullying and fear of judgement can make it challenging to express one's identity openly.

The stories in the book highlight why acceptance matters. People should not have to hide parts of themselves to fit into a workplace or earn respect.

True inclusion begins when individuals are welcomed for who they are, without being expected to change their identities to meet someone else's expectations.

2. Everyone deserves to feel safe and valued at work

A workplace is more than a place where people earn a living. It is also where they spend a significant part of their lives, build relationships and develop their confidence.

Through the experiences of queer employees at The LaLiT, the book highlights the importance of creating environments where people can work without constantly worrying about discrimination or judgement.

It also reflects an important realisation in the organisation's inclusion journey: hiring people from marginalised communities is only the beginning. Organisations must also establish systems, policies and support structures that allow employees to feel protected and respected.

A truly inclusive workplace is one where everyone has the opportunity to grow without compromising their sense of identity.

3. Empathy can change the way we see others

People often form opinions about others without understanding the experiences they have lived through.

Hospitality with a Heart encourages readers to look beyond assumptions and recognise the human stories behind individual identities.

The experiences shared in the book include isolation, societal pressure, bullying and the struggle to find acceptance. These stories remind readers that everyone carries experiences that may not be immediately visible.

Empathy begins when we make an effort to listen instead of judge. By understanding another person's journey, we can build stronger relationships and create communities where differences are respected rather than questioned.

Also Read
5 Books you must add to your November 2026 reading list

4. Every individual story deserves to be heard

Representation is important because it allows people to see their experiences acknowledged rather than overlooked.

The book brings together the personal journeys of queer team members whose stories reflect different struggles, milestones and experiences. By documenting their voices, Amrita Tripathi creates space for conversations that are often missing from mainstream narratives.

Sharing these experiences also challenges stereotypes and helps readers understand the realities faced by people from marginalised communities.

The lesson is simple: listening to people and giving them the space to tell their stories can help build understanding. Every individual deserves to have their experiences recognised, respected and heard.

5. Belonging is built through everyday actions

Perhaps the most meaningful lesson from Hospitality with a Heart is that belonging cannot be created through statements or policies alone. It is built through everyday actions.

An inclusive environment requires consistent efforts from leadership, colleagues and the wider organisation. It means treating everyone with dignity, challenging discriminatory behaviour, listening to different perspectives and ensuring that people feel comfortable being themselves.

The LaLiT's inclusion journey, as documented in the book, highlights the importance of moving beyond representation towards meaningful acceptance.

Whether in a workplace, a community or personal relationships, making someone feel that they belong is an ongoing responsibility.

Final thoughts

Hospitality with a Heart by Amrita Tripathi is a reminder that behind every conversation about diversity and inclusion are real people with individual stories, struggles and aspirations.

By documenting the lived experiences of queer employees at The LaLiT, the book explores what it means to move from representation to acceptance and from employment to genuine belonging.

The October 31 launch brought these ideas into focus through conversations involving the author, the organisation's leadership, speakers and the people whose experiences form the heart of the book.

Ultimately, the book leaves readers with an important thought: hospitality should not end with welcoming someone through the door. It should extend to making them feel respected, accepted and at home.

item.title: Neha Nagar wants to help people take control of their financial future through her debut book
item.description: 'Simple Money Serious Wealth', which sold over 3,000 copies on launch day, is another feather in the cap of this popular finance educator and content creator.
item.content:encoded:
Finance educator and content creator Neha Nagar recently launched her debut book Simple Money Serious Wealth: How to Turn Ordinary Income into Extraordinary Net Worth. 

Neha, who has been in the finance field for over a decade and in content creation for about seven years, decided to don the role of an author when she realised that, while people in India know more about money today than earlier, they aren’t necessarily good at managing it. 

“Almost everyone has watched a video on SIPs, insurance or tax-saving. They have information, but they don't have a structure. People start investing with excitement, but when markets fall or an unexpected expense comes up, they stop. Often, it's because they never had a plan behind that investment,” Neha tells YourStory.  

While a social media platform helps disseminate information, it has its structural limitations. A book, on the other hand, gives the author the space to explain an entire concept elaborately. 

“We wanted to help people build their own financial plan, choose products that actually suit their lives, and understand how to structure their money better. For me, social media can introduce people to money. But this book is about teaching them how to manage it,” says the New Delhi-based author. 

Her debut book Simple Money Serious Wealth was published on October 24. It sold over 3,000 copies in the first 24 hours, according to a post on the author's Instagram account. 

“At a bookstore in the city, we saw people in the 60–70 years age group picking up the book. Some were buying it for themselves, while others wanted it for their children and grandchildren. We also saw students, young professionals, working women, and parents,” she says. 

Also Read
How Neha Nagar is demystifying personal finance through simple content

Educating a nation of billions

While embarking upon the book project, Neha thought that having explained finance through videos for seven years, writing a book would be a piece of cake. But she soon realised that was not the case. 

“A book has to work even when the author isn’t around. In my videos, if someone doesn't understand something, they can leave a comment and I can respond. But when someone is reading a book alone, every step has to be clear,” says Neha, who was recognised by Hurun India as India's most-followed female personal finance influencer in 2025. 

The creator-turned-author believes India is still far away from reaching financial literacy. There are many reasons for this, she says.  

One, our education system never teaches students how to manage salary, calculate insurance requirements, save taxes, or plan for retirement. 

The second reason is that money isn’t discussed openly in many Indian households. “So, one goes from never being made aware of finance to suddenly stumbling upon an information overload on social media. That transition makes it very hard for people to identify needful information from noise,” she elaborates.

Also Read
Beyond assets: Why 'family continuity' is the missing link in personal finance

The ultimate reason is fear, says Neha. Many Indians still associate the stock market with gambling. Due to this notion, they do not make attempts to understand different investment options, and a lot of money remains in savings accounts without a clear purpose.

“My goal with Simple Money Serious Wealth is to help people understand their own money, make informed decisions, and take control of their financial future. Because financial independence isn’t just about how much you earn; it’s about how confidently you can manage what you earn,” she says.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: How Bout India built a travel company without selling packages
item.description:
By refusing the cookie‑cutter tour, Himanshu Maru and his co‑founders turned personalization into a moat, earning 970+ glowing reviews and a loyal global clientele.
Himanshu Maru started Bout India in 2013 with a simple bet: that international travellers to India wanted something built around t
item.content:encoded:
Himanshu Maru started Bout India in 2013 with a simple bet: that international travellers to India wanted something built around them, not a fixed itinerary sold off a brochure. Thirteen years later, that bet has become the foundation of a distinctive inbound travel business.

Most travel companies begin by asking how many packages they can sell. Bout India took a different route. Founded in Jaipur in 2013 by Himanshu Maru, Managing Director; Bhupender Rana, Director, Operations; and Vinod Jhajharia, Director, Marketing, the company built its offering around a simple proposition: international travellers visiting India should not have to fit themselves into a pre-designed itinerary.

Each journey is planned around the traveller’s interests, pace and practical requirements. The company’s model centers on 100% tailor-made trips, with no fixed group packages and a direct relationship between the traveller and the person responsible for planning the experience.

Why tailor‑made mattered more than packages

Planning a trip to India can be complex for a first-time international visitor. The country’s geographic scale, distinct cultural regions, transport options, and local logistics require decisions that go beyond booking flights and hotels.

A traveller interested in Rajasthan may want heritage sites and local experiences, while someone visiting Ladakh may need planning around altitude, road conditions, and acclimatization. A wellness traveller heading to Kerala may prioritize retreat quality and time for rest.

Maru’s founding insight was that travellers would value a company that removed this complexity while preserving the feeling that the journey belonged to them. Rather than selling a standard route, Bout India positioned itself as a planning partner.

That approach is reflected in the company’s Destination Expert model. Each client is assigned a named expert who manages the relationship from the initial enquiry through the trip.

Reviews published on the company’s website frequently mention individual team members by name. While testimonials are not independent audits of service quality, this pattern illustrates the personal accountability the company seeks to build into its operating model.

Zero negative reviews and repeat travellers According to Bout India’s reported company information, its traction includes:

  • 4.9/5-stars average rating across 970+ reviews on TripAdvisor and Google Maps
  • A claimed zero-negative-review and 100% happy-customer record
  • Travellers served from over 50 countries
  • References to repeat customers who have booked second or third trips

The distinction between company-reported claims and independently verified performance is important. Review platforms can change, ratings can fluctuate, and customer-satisfaction records should ideally be assessed through the underlying reviews. Nevertheless, the reported figures indicate the reputation Bout India has sought to build.

For a services business, repeat and referral behavior can be especially valuable. A returning traveller is placing trust in the company’s ability to understand their preferences and deliver consistently.

Keeping personal involvement at the core

Bout India’s positioning continues to emphasize founder involvement. Company testimonials reference Maru personally checking in with clients, responding to concerns, and remaining involved in the travel experience.

Its Destination Expert structure combines individual ownership with a broader team. The company has also expanded across categories, including heritage travel, luxury experiences, wellness and Ayurveda retreats in Kerala, high-altitude adventure travel in Ladakh and Spiti, wildlife safaris, spiritual circuits, honeymoon and family travel, and corporate/MICE travel.

Why bespoke journeys beat standardized tours

Bout India’s model reflects a broader shift in the experience economy. As travellers gain access to online booking platforms and standardized packages, the value of a specialist may increasingly lie in interpretation, judgement, and reassurance.

A booking platform can compare prices, but a specialist can help a traveller decide whether a route is realistic, whether a destination suits their interests, or how to balance sightseeing with rest.

That is particularly relevant to inbound travel, where customers may be unfamiliar with local distances, seasonal conditions and operational realities. A tailor-made approach can address those concerns before they become problems.

Personalized travel does require skilled staff, detailed communication, and careful execution. The company must, therefore, demonstrate that the additional service creates enough value to justify the model.

Lessons in trust, service, and differentiation

Bout India is not a technology startup in the traditional sense. Its core proposition is built around people, destination expertise, and service delivery. Yet its approach offers a lesson relevant to India’s wider services economy.

In high-trust, high-consideration purchases such as international travel, radical personalization can be a durable differentiator. Customers may compare prices, but they also evaluate how confidently a company understands their needs and responds when plans change.

For founders, the lesson is to identify which parts of the customer experience should remain personal as the business grows. Technology can improve communication and operations, but the underlying relationship still depends on judgement and accountability.

Bout India’s journey illustrates one possible answer: build a system in which personal attention is not an exception, but a defining part of the product itself.

(Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

item.title: 3 Books to read instead of doomscrolling every day
item.description: Replace endless scrolling with meaningful reading. Discover three books that can help you reclaim your attention & build healthier digital habits.
item.content:encoded:
How often do you pick up your phone to check one notification and end up spending the next hour scrolling through Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts or endless social media updates?

Doomscrolling has quietly become part of everyday life. What begins as a few minutes of entertainment can turn into hours of consuming content without much thought or purpose. While social media keeps us occupied, it can also leave us feeling distracted, mentally exhausted and dissatisfied.

One way to break this habit is to replace mindless scrolling with something that adds value to your life. Reading is a great place to start. Even dedicating 15–20 minutes a day to a good book can help you develop new perspectives, improve your focus, and use your free time better.

If you are looking for a reason to put your phone down, here are three books worth adding to your reading list.

3 Books to read instead of doomscrolling every day

1. Digital Minimalism by Cal Newport

If you constantly find yourself checking your phone without a specific reason, Digital Minimalism is a good place to begin.

In this book, Cal Newport introduces the idea of using technology intentionally rather than allowing it to dictate how you spend your time. He explains that digital minimalism is not about abandoning technology altogether. Instead, it involves identifying which digital tools genuinely add value to your life and reducing the ones that create unnecessary distractions.

One of the book's key ideas is a 30-day digital declutter, which encourages readers to step away from optional digital activities and gradually reintroduce only those that serve a meaningful purpose.

Why you should read it: This book can help you rethink your relationship with social media, set healthier boundaries with your phone and make more room for activities that genuinely matter.

2. Stolen Focus by Johann Hari

Have you ever opened an app for a few minutes, only to realise that an entire hour has passed? Or found yourself switching between multiple tabs while struggling to finish a simple task?

Stolen Focus explores the growing attention crisis and the factors that make it difficult for people to concentrate. Johann Hari investigates how technology, constant interruptions, information overload and other aspects of modern life affect our ability to pay attention.

Rather than blaming individuals for having poor self-control, the author examines the wider systems and habits that contribute to distracted living.

Why you should read it: If you want to understand why doomscrolling and constant notifications make it difficult to focus, this book offers an insightful look at the problem and how we can begin reclaiming our attention.

3. How to Break Up with Your Phone by Catherine Price

If you have tried reducing your screen time but keep returning to the same scrolling habits, this book offers a practical starting point.

How to Break Up with Your Phone explores how smartphones influence our attention, daily routines and relationships. Catherine Price encourages readers to examine their phone habits and understand what keeps them reaching for their devices.

The book offers a 30-day plan designed to help readers develop a healthier relationship with their phones. Instead of asking you to give up technology completely, it focuses on making more conscious choices about when and why you use it.

Why you should read it: This is a useful choice if you want practical steps to reduce unnecessary screen time, build better habits and spend more time enjoying life away from a screen.

Also Read
5 lessons from 30 Something Millionaire by Mohit Chawla

Final thoughts

Doomscrolling can make us feel occupied without necessarily making our lives more meaningful. We consume hundreds of posts, watch countless videos and follow endless updates, yet often struggle to remember what we actually gained from all that screen time.

These three books offer different ways to understand and address the problem. While Digital Minimalism helps you use technology more intentionally, Stolen Focus explores why our attention is constantly under pressure, and How to Break Up with Your Phone offers practical steps to change your habits.

You do not have to stop using social media completely. Start by replacing just 15 minutes of scrolling with reading every day. Over time, that small change can help you build a more intentional and fulfilling routine.

item.title: Arka Fincap raises Rs 525 Cr from The Rise Funds of TPG
item.description:
Arka Fincap was founded in 2018
Arka Fincap will use this capital for expansion, investments into technology and risk management capabilities
Arka Fincap Limited, a Kirloskar Group-promoted non-banking financial company (NBFC) has raised an initial investment of Rs 525 crore from The Rise Funds,
item.content:encoded:
Arka Fincap Limited, a Kirloskar Group-promoted non-banking financial company (NBFC) recently raised an initial investment of Rs 525 crore from The Rise Funds, the global impact investing arm of TPG.

A statement said this agreement could also lead to an additional Rs 275 crore through a subsequent tranche, subject to the achievement of specified business milestones aligned with Arka’s growth strategy and requisite regulatory approvals.

The investment from TPG will provide growth capital for Arka to expand its geographical reach and accelerate investments in technology and risk management capabilities.

Founded in 2018, Arka is a diversified retail lending institution with an assets under management (AUM) of over Rs 8,000 crore and a presence across ten states through 146 branches.

On the funds raised, Gauri Kirloskar, Vice Chairperson and Managing Director, Kirloskar Oil Engines Limited, said “As a Group, we have always placed great value on enduring partnerships and the institution-building ethos of creating businesses that stand the test of time. We seek partners who share this philosophy, and we see a strong alignment with TPG’s approach.”

Arka offers a diversified portfolio of financing solutions spanning pre-owned vehicle financing, secured business loans, loan against property and wholesale lending. The company serves entrepreneurs, MSMEs, vehicle operators and corporate clients through a combination of specialised lending businesses and a growing distribution network.

Samrat Gupta, Managing Director, Arka Fincap Limited, said, “Crossing Rs 1,000 crore in secured retail assets is a defining milestone in our ambition to build a formidable, future-ready financial enterprise, serving entrepreneurial aspirations of our country.”

Simit Batra, BU Partner, TPG, said, “Many of India’s MSMEs and vehicle operators remain underserved by formal financial services, and Arka has built a disciplined, secured retail lending platform to serve these customers, with the potential to reach even more customers at scale.”

Founded in 2016 by TPG in partnership with Bono and Jeff Skoll, The Rise Funds invest behind impact entrepreneurs and growth-stage, high-potential companies.

item.title: MakeMyTrip's India arm gets Sebi nod to float IPO
item.description:
MakeMyTrip is listed on Nasdaq stock exchange
The proceeds from the planned IPO will be utilised by MakeMyTrip for long term growth, inorganic opportunities and repurchase of different types shares
Nasdaq-listed travel booking platform MakeMyTrip's India subsidiary has received Sebi's approval to
item.content:encoded:
Nasdaq-listed travel booking platform MakeMyTrip's India subsidiary has received Sebi's approval to launch an initial public offering (IPO), according to an update available on the markets regulator's website.

MakeMyTrip (India) Ltd (MMT India) had filed draft papers with Sebi in July through the confidential route. After examining the draft documents, the regulator issued its final observations on November 6.

Sebi's observations mark an important step in the IPO process, allowing the company to proceed with preparations for its public issues, subject to applicable regulatory requirements.

The proposed IPO is expected to comprise a sale of equity shares in MMT India by its parent MakeMyTrip and its wholly-owned subsidiary, ibibo Group Holdings (Singapore) Pte Ltd, the Gurugram-headquartered company said in a regulatory filing with Nasdaq.

Following the completion of the proposed IPO, MMT India will continue to remain a subsidiary of MakeMyTrip, with its financial results continuing to be consolidated with those of the parent company, it had said.

"MakeMyTrip expects the proposed initial public offering and listing of MMT India to enhance its brand visibility and support MMT India's ability to incentivise and promote talent in a competitive technology recruitment landscape," the filing stated.

The net proceeds received by MakeMyTrip and ibibo Group Holdings from the sale of shares in MMT India are expected to strengthen the parent's cash position.

The proceeds will be utilised for long-term growth, strategic inorganic initiatives and repurchases of different classes of securities, including convertible securities, by MakeMyTrip, the filing stated.

MakeMyTrip swung back into profit for the three months ending September, 2026 boosted by increased booking across all categories. The company reported a net profit of $1.8 million for the second quarter of FY27 as compared to loss of $5.7 million in the similar period a year ago. The revenue for the second quarter touched $235.2 million which was a 11.2% increase when compared to the similar period of last fiscal.

item.title: Private scandals that derailed tech execs’ careers; Neha Nagar’s new book on helping people invest
item.description: Executive exits can result from violations of company policies, even when no criminal wrongdoing has been established. Brian Krzanich resigned from Intel over a consensual subordinate relationship, while Phaneesh Murthy was dismissed by iGate for failing to disclose a relationship.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

Anthropic has launched the roadshow for its blockbuster IPO, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. The Claude maker aims to raise as much as $64.4 billion through the share sale, in what could become one of the largest public offerings in history. The proposed valuation comes amid growing investor scrutiny of the enormous costs of building AI infrastructure.

The controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has raised questions about succession planning at the AI chip giant. Valued at around $4 trillion, Nvidia faces a difficult question: Who could eventually succeed the executive who built it into an AI powerhouse?

OpenAI has unveiled Control Room, which is a rapid-response kill switch designed to pull the plug on rogue AI workloads and safety threats in under 35 seconds. Control Room will be a central system to track model workloads across the research infrastructure of OpenAI.

Closer home, the board of IIFL Finance has greenlit a massive Rs 6,414 crore ($686 million) primary capital raise, headlined by private equity heavyweight Blackstone. In what marks one of the largest PE infusions into a listed Indian NBFC, Blackstone is committing Rs 5,000 crore ($535 million) via compulsorily convertible preference shares. The instruments will convert at Rs 602 per share within 18 months, handing the firm a roughly 16% stake on a fully diluted basis.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Private scandals that derailed tech execs’ careers
  • Neha Nagar’s new book on helping people invest

Here’s your trivia for today: Which arcade gaming pioneer founded by Nolan Bushnell took its name from a Japanese board game term equivalent to "check" in chess? (Scroll down for answer)

Technology

Private scandals that derailed tech execs’ careers

Several prominent tech leaders have seen their careers interrupted or upended by personal conduct and relationship controversies rather than operational failures. The scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang mirrors past high-profile executive cases across global tech and Indian startups. 

While the nature of the allegations ranges from undisclosed consensual relationships to sexual harassment claims, these incidents consistently trigger governance reviews, leadership transitions, and broader scrutiny of corporate culture.

Key takeaways:

  • Executive exits can result from violations of company policies, even when no criminal wrongdoing has been established. Brian Krzanich resigned from Intel over a consensual subordinate relationship, while Phaneesh Murthy was dismissed by iGate for failing to disclose a relationship.
  • Severe misconduct fallout can prompt broad organisational issues, as seen in the protests at Google in 2018 following reports of a $90 million payout to Android creator Andy Rubin amid credible misconduct findings.
  • Legal outcomes vary significantly across cases; TVF founder Arunabh Kumar stepped down amid allegations in 2017 but was fully acquitted by a court in 2022 due to lack of evidence.

Inspiration

Neha Nagar’s new book on helping people invest

Earning money is not the same as managing it. In her book, Simple Money Serious Wealth: How to Turn Ordinary Income into Extraordinary Net Worth, Neha Nagar provides an investment structure for readers.

While a social media platform helps disseminate information, it has its structural limitations. A book, on the other hand, gives the author the space to explain an entire concept elaborately. 

Key takeaways:

  • Her debut book Simple Money Serious Wealth was published on October 24. It sold over 3,000 copies in the first 24 hours, according to a post on the author's Instagram account. 
  • The creator-turned-author believes India is still far away from reaching financial literacy. There are many reasons for this, she says.  
  • Fear stops many people from exploring investment strategies, Neha says, as many Indians still associate the stock market with gambling.

News & updates

  • Startup awards: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade has opened applications for the sixth edition of the National Startup Awards, offering a prize of Rs 25 lakh in each category to recognise innovative, scalable and impactful startups across the country.
  • Fundraising: Arka Fincap Limited, a Kirloskar Group-promoted non-banking financial company has raised an initial investment of Rs 525 crore from The Rise Funds, the global impact investing arm of TPG.
  • Jobs moving to India: Australian airline Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India. The move comes amid the company’s AI push. 

Which arcade gaming pioneer founded by Nolan Bushnell took its name from a Japanese board game term equivalent to "check" in chess?

Answer: Atari

item.title: With Jensen Huang under fire, Nvidia looks at sucession plans
item.description: The controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s improper relationship with a Chinese citizen has raised national security concerns for the US.
item.content:encoded:
The controversy surrounding Nvidia founder & CEO Jensen Huang has raised questions about the future leadership and succession planning at the company. At $4 trillion, the chipmaker is second only to Apple in terms of valuation.

A report in the The Wall Street Journal says that Huang runs a very flat leadership structure with about 60 direct reportees and there is no visible second rung of leadership or any potential successors in the company.

This has become an important question for Nvidia as Huang will come under increased scrutiny for his improper relationship with a Chinese national Alice Huang, who is allegedly a spy for the Chinese government. This relationship supposedly enabled China to get access to the high-end processors of Nvidia.

Also, reports quoting United States President Donald Trump said that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is looking into the relationship between the Nvidia CEO and the Chinese national. Trump has defended Huang as a very "honorable" man.

In addition, the US Congress will also come into the picture seeking information on the kind of relationship and whether any sensitive technology has been passed onto China bypassing regulation.

However, reports also quoting an Nvidia spokesperson said, Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.

The Board of Nvidia has already stated that it would be investigating the entire matter.

The leadership question comes into picture as there is the angle of national security with regard to the CEO’s relationship with the Chinese citizen and this brings the government into the picture. This is not a leadership crisis which a corporate typically faces where the issues are generally around business challenges, shareholder dissatisfaction, and physical health of the CEO.

Jensen Huang has built a larger-than-life picture not just for Nvidia but also for the AI world. He is seen as an influential individual determining the contours of any new policy with regard to the AI industry. Along with this, he is also well networked with the various heads of States across the globe.

Though, it must be noted that both his children, Madison Huang and Spencer Huang work at Nvidia. Additionally, his son-in-law Nico Caprez also works with the company.

At this point of time, it is difficult to gauge the future direction of Nvidia as there are several elements in play. The improper relationship is one aspect, the bigger repercussion is whether technology was illegally acquired by a foreign country.

Although at the same time, some industry watchers see it as a proxy fight between the United States and China to gain the upper hand in the world of AI. China is seen as being close to matching the technology prowess of the United States and potentially overtaking it.

item.title: Nvidia probes whether foreign intelligence targeted Jensen Huang
item.description: Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The company has said its board had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security had been compromised.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Readers,

Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The move follows a New York Times report alleging that a business executive with whom Huang had a close relationship passed information to Beijing.

The company shares slid sharply on Monday following this news. 

Nvidia said its board had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security had been compromised.

In other news, Sashikumar Sreedharan, the former MD for India at Google Cloud, has joined AI company Sarvam as President and Chief Business Officer. He will also be on the company’s board. Sreedharan will run Sarvam’s business across enterprises and government and expand its work with digital-native companies, developers and partners.

Meanwhile, the India subsidiary of travel booking platform MakeMyTrip has received Sebi’s approval to launch an initial public offering (IPO). The proposed IPO is expected to comprise a sale of equity shares in MMT India by its parent MakeMyTrip and its wholly-owned subsidiary, ibibo Group Holdings (Singapore) Pte Ltd. 

Lastly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record, according to the World Meteorological Organization.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • How Bariflo uses AI to help factories treat wastewater
  • How these Mothers of Courage are fighting to keep girls in school

Here’s your trivia for today: What was Henry Ford’s original design for a car called? (Scroll down for the answer)

In-focus

How Bariflo uses AI to help factories treat wastewater

Bariflo Cybernetics wants factories to get more use out of their wastewater treatment plants. The Odisha-based startup combines sensors, AI software, and automation to adjust treatment processes, aiming to reduce the energy and chemicals needed to clean water for reuse. 

It recently secured Rs 2 crore in milestone-linked funding from energy innovation platform MC² Plus, an initiative led by the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas, and is preparing for a pilot with Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), according to founder and CEO Mrityunjay Sahu. The funding comes as Bariflo moves from developing and testing its technology towards commercial deployments. That means persuading industrial customers to invest in upgrades that promise lower operating costs.

Key takeaways 

  • Founded in 2018, Bariflo initially focused on monitoring and cleaning municipal waterbodies. It subsequently explored aquaculture, including shrimp and fish farming, before concentrating on industrial wastewater treatment and reuse. It is now engaged in making existing treatment infrastructure smarter and more efficient. 
  • Bariflo’s proprietary IoT sensors monitor wastewater parameters such as pH, total dissolved solids, and flow. Its AI models use the readings to determine chemical dosage and treatment processes at different stages. This automates some decisions that operators would otherwise make manually and helps plants respond as the characteristics of incoming wastewater change. 
  • The company has conducted pilots with Indian Oil Corporation’s R&D centre in Faridabad. Its planned BPCL pilot will test treatment efficiency, energy consumption, and chemical use in an industrial setting. Founder Sahu hopes successful validation will pave the way for a commercial work order. 

Social impact

How these Mothers of Courage are fighting to keep girls in school 

Mothers of Courage, a documentary on girls’ education in Bihar, recently won the 2026 UN SDG Action Award in the Creativity category. It captures how women in rural Bihar are challenging social norms to keep girls in school.

Directed by Vandana R Jaikumar and produced by Butterfly Effect Media, the documentary was chosen from more than 7,000 applications from 190 countries and territories. 

Key takeaways 

  • In rural Bihar, mothers are at the centre of a quiet revolution. They are negotiating with their families so their daughters can keep studying. Others are standing up for daughters-in-law who want to return to school. This quiet, stubborn conviction and resilience is the subject of the documentary.
  • Mothers of Courage is part of Shikshagraha, a national movement to strengthen public education championed by Infosys Co-founder and former CEO S D Shibulal, and supported by Bengaluru-based non-profits ShikshaLokam and Mantra4Change.
  • Urmila Kumari, State Head for Shikshagraha in Bihar, is the living embodiment of the movement. She has spent nearly three decades working for the rights and education of girls and young women. She says the UN recognition belongs to “thousands of women and adolescent girls whose courage and determination have driven the fight for girls' education and rights.”

News & updates

  • New GCC: SplashBI, a Georgia (US)-headquartered enterprise data intelligence platform, has opened its global capability centre in Hyderabad. The company plans to invest over $100 million over five to seven years in infrastructure, technology and talent to scale the Hyderabad centre and strengthen its global product engineering and delivery capabilities. 
  • Age checks: Meta Platforms plans to expand its AI age-estimation technology globally to move millions more teens on Instagram ​into Teen Account protections, even if they have given ‌birth dates showing they are adults. This comes as the company faces lawsuits alleging its platforms harm young users.
  • AI guardrails: US President Donald Trump said the ​risks posed by artificial intelligence ‌can be managed but signalled an openness to safeguards, telling CBS’s 60 Minutes ​that he “doesn’t mind guardrails.”

What was Henry Ford’s original design for a car called?

Answer: Quadricycle

item.title: National Startup Awards 6.0 opens applications; winners to receive Rs 25 lakh prize in 20 categories
item.description: The award exercise seeks to identify and recognise entrepreneurial ventures that make significant contributions across 20 sectoral categories, from agriculture to space technology.
item.content:encoded:
The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) has opened applications for the sixth edition of the National Startup Awards, offering a prize of Rs 25 lakh in each category to recognise innovative, scalable and impactful startups across the country.

These awards recognise startups demonstrating outstanding performance in innovation, scalability, sustainability and socio-economic impact, according to DPIIT.

The award exercise is organised under the Startup India initiative of the commerce and industry ministry. It seeks to identify and recognise entrepreneurial ventures making significant contributions across 20 sectoral categories, spanning areas from agriculture to space technology.

The awards also include special categories for women-led startups, North-East Startup Excellence, student innovators, and aspiring entrepreneurs.

This exercise will provide national-level visibility and recognition to selected startups, while also facilitating access to industry stakeholders and potential investors.

Further, the DPIIT-recognised startups are eligible to apply for these awards under the 20 sectoral categories and the specified special categories. Over 2.6 lakh units are recognised as startups by the department.

Students aged 10 and above can also submit applications for the award, provided their proposed solutions align with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 and 'Shakti Ki Sapta Dhara'.

On August 15, Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid out a seven-point reform framework, 'Sapta Dhara', aimed at accelerating India's journey towards becoming a developed nation by 2047, with a focus on manufacturing, agro-food production and food processing, technology and innovation, logistics, defence, green and blue economy, and soft power.

Interested applicants can submit their applications through the Startup India portal at https://www.startupindia.gov.in/content/sih/en/nsa2026.html.

item.title: From conversations to action: How Cogover is addressing commitment leakage in Indian enterprises
item.description: Selected for NetApp Excellerator, Cogover is connecting customer conversations, business workflows, and AI agents to help enterprises turn commitments into accountable action.
item.content:encoded:
At 11 am, a borrower tells a collections agent they will make a payment on Friday. The conversation is recorded, the agent moves to the next call, and the account may be handled by someone else days later. When Friday arrives, does the team know what was promised, who owns the follow-up, and whether payment was received?

This is the problem Cogover calls ‘commitment leakage’: customer commitments that lose context, ownership, or follow-through as work moves between people and disconnected systems.

For Indian enterprises managing large volumes of calls, approvals and customer requests, the cost is not simply missed tasks. It is repeated conversations, delayed resolutions, and limited visibility into whether work actually gets done.

The gap between a conversation and an outcome

Most enterprises already have tools to store customer records, manage calls, and track tasks. The difficulty arises when employees must manually connect them.

In lending, a promise-to-pay may be recorded without a clear next action. In brokerage, a customer seeking help with KYC can wait while teams coordinate. In real estate, a promised site visit may never become a confirmed appointment.

Managers can see call volumes but may struggle to identify unresolved commitments. Employees piece together notes and messages, while customers repeat information they have already shared.

Cogover is addressing that operational gap with an Agentic Enterprise Platform that brings CRM, built-in calling, workflows, and AI agents into one environment. Its central proposition is straightforward: a customer interaction should lead to a visible, accountable next step.

What makes the approach agentic?

An AI summary can save time, but it does not by itself assign an owner, approve an exception, or ensure a follow-up happens.

In Cogover, AI agents are designed to participate in defined business processes. They can help extract information from a conversation, propose a record update or prepare a task. Permissions and workflow rules determine what can proceed automatically and what requires human review.

Because calling is built into the same platform, an employee can dial from a customer record and access the relevant history, disposition, and subsequent work without moving between separate tools. A supervisor reviewing an exception can trace a task back to its originating interaction.

The goal is not to replace employee judgment. It is to make the context, responsibility, and next action available to the right person at the right time.

A promise-to-pay, followed through

Consider a collections workflow. An agent calls a borrower from the account record. AI helps identify the proposed amount, payment date and intent. The employee checks those details before confirming the commitment.

The workflow then assigns a follow-up with an owner and deadline. If the borrower requests an arrangement beyond the agent’s authority, the request moves to an approver with the conversation context attached. If a relevant payment-status integration is available, that update can guide the next action.

When a deadline passes, the unresolved item becomes visible to the responsible supervisor instead of disappearing into personal notes.

Crucially, the process distinguishes what the customer promised, what the employee must do, and whether the business outcome occurred. A completed follow-up is not the same as a received payment. Both need to be measurable.

The same design can support brokerage KYC resolution, real-estate site-visit coordination and service escalations, each with its own ownership, approval and exception rules.

Building around real enterprise processes

Enterprise workflows rarely match a rigid template. An approval may depend on transaction value, customer type, or branch. A service exception might involve sales, operations, and finance.

Cogover combines AI-assisted application creation with low-code configuration so teams can shape fields, stages, permissions, and escalation paths around those realities. They can review an initial working application and refine it against actual cases rather than relying solely on a static specification.

That flexibility matters in enterprises where formal systems coexist with conversations, messaging and cross-functional decisions. To operate reliably, those informal handoffs must become explicit business rules.

Why NetApp Excellerator matters

Cogover’s selection for NetApp Excellerator creates an opportunity to connect this application-led approach with a broader enterprise data perspective.

One customer request may depend on a recording, CRM history, an approval policy and a transaction update. For AI to assist responsibly, it needs relevant data and controlled access. For the organization to trust the process, actions need ownership and traceability.

NetApp brings an enterprise data infrastructure perspective; Cogover brings the customer interactions and operational workflows where data is translated into decisions and actions. Participation in the program provides a setting to explore that connection further.

Measure actions, not just activity

For businesses evaluating agentic AI, Cogover suggests starting with a specific workflow rather than a broad automation target.

Can managers identify every commitment made yesterday and its owner? Can approvers access the original context? How many follow-ups are overdue? How often must customers call again for an update?

A focused pilot can measure ownership coverage, approval turnaround, missed deadlines, repeated data entry, and customer follow-up rates. Teams should also monitor errors and human corrections, not merely processing speed.

For simple, low-volume work, shared task tracking may be sufficient. As customer interactions, handoffs, and approvals multiply, a connected system becomes more valuable.

Cogover’s argument is that enterprise AI delivers practical value when it moves beyond generating information to helping people complete work with clear permissions, accountability, and evidence of outcomes.

item.title: IIFL Finance to raise Rs 6,414 Cr led by Blackstone
item.description: Promoters to put in Rs 1,264 crore through warrants; capital adequacy to rise to about 30%
item.content:encoded:
IIFL Finance has approved a Rs 6,414 crore ($686 million) primary capital raise, with Blackstone leading the round.

The board cleared the preferential issue at a meeting on Tuesday. The deal is one of the largest primary private equity infusions in a listed Indian non-banking finance company, according to IIFL.

Funds managed by Blackstone Private Equity will invest Rs 5,000 crore ($535 million) in compulsorily convertible preference shares, which will convert into equity at Rs 602 a share, in line with the regulatory price, within 18 months of allotment. The company said this would give Blackstone a stake of about 16 % on a fully diluted basis.

The promoters, Nirmal Jain and R. Venkataraman, will invest Rs 1,264 crore (135 million) through a preferential allotment of warrants, and will continue as co-promoters. Anchorage Capital is also participating, with a Rs 150 crore (16 million) primary equity investment. The company and its promoters have signed definitive agreements with both investors.

IIFL Finance said the entire sum will go in as primary capital. On a pro forma basis for September 2026, which would lift its capital adequacy ratio from roughly 17% to roughly 30%. The company said the money would support growth in its secured lending businesses, particularly gold finance, and could, over time, improve its credit ratings and lower its borrowing costs.

Nirmal Jain, founder and managing director of IIFL Finance, said: “We are delighted to welcome Blackstone as a partner in IIFL Finance. Their investment is a strong endorsement of the franchise our team has built, and of the opportunity to bring formal, secured credit to millions of underserved households and small businesses across India. Venkat and I are investing Rs 1,264 crores alongside Blackstone, which reflects our own conviction in the Company’s next phase of growth.

“This partnership is about more than capital. Blackstone brings deep experience in building market-leading businesses in India, strong governance discipline, and a global perspective. The investment strengthens our balance sheet and gives us the headroom to scale our franchises, invest further in technology, and deepen our co-lending partnerships with banks, while staying disciplined on risk and capital.”

IIFL Finance also expects to draw on Blackstone’s global network and operational expertise, including in technology, data and artificial intelligence. Blackstone representatives are proposed to join the board, which the company said would strengthen governance while preserving its entrepreneurial culture.

Mukesh Mehta, chief investment officer for India private equity and senior managing director at Blackstone, said: “We are pleased to invest in IIFL Finance, a leading retail lending platform in India with a strong franchise and commitment to serving underserved customers. Building great businesses has been central to our approach over more than two decades of investing in India, and we look forward to partnering with Nirmal, Venkat and the management team to support IIFL Finance’s continued growth.”

The transaction remains subject to customary regulatory and shareholder approvals. Trilegal advised IIFL Finance, while Khaitan & Co advised Blackstone.

IIFL Finance offers gold, business, home and microfinance loans, among other products, through 5,091 branches across urban and rural India. Blackstone, which says it manages nearly $1.4 trillion in assets, has been investing in India for 20 years."

item.title: SplashBI opens GCC in Hyderabad, to invest over $100M
item.description:
The investment to be spread across 5 years
The GCC of SplashBI will strengthen the company’s product engineering and delivery capabilities
SplashBI, a Georgia (US)-headquartered enterprise data intelligence platform, opened its global capability centre (GCC) in Hyderabad.
The company plans to i
item.content:encoded:
SplashBI, a Georgia (US)-headquartered enterprise data intelligence platform, has opened its global capability centre (GCC) in Hyderabad.

The company plans to invest over $100 million over the next five to seven years in infrastructure, technology and talent to scale the Hyderabad centre and strengthen its global product engineering and delivery capabilities, a release said.

The 20,000-square-foot facility, with capacity for 275 professionals, was inaugurated by Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu.

SplashBI has had a presence in Hyderabad since 2014. The new facility brings its teams in the city together under one roof, designed to support collaboration and growth, the release said.

The centre will support the development of SplashBI’s data intelligence platform and global customer delivery, helping enterprises connect business data, establish shared business context and use that data for decisions, AI, analytics and reporting, it said.

Platform engineering, AI development, domain analytics and customer delivery teams will work closely together at the Global Capability Center, the release said.

They will work on data connectivity and business modelling, develop SplashAI capabilities and support customer implementations.

“Enterprises need a practical way to turn the data they already have into decisions they can trust. That requires understanding how their business works, connecting information across functions and giving people useful ways to explore it,” said Naveen Miglani, CEO and Co-Founder of SplashBI.

“Our Hyderabad centre strengthens the engineering and customer expertise behind that work, as we help customers advance their data foundations and adopt AI with the right business context,” he added.

Kiran Reddy Pasham, President and Co-Founder of SplashBI, said, “Our teams in Hyderabad will build the platform capabilities and domain content that help customers connect their data, make sense of it and use it in their everyday work.”

item.title: 5 tech and startup leaders whose personal scandals shook their careers
item.description: As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces scrutiny over an extramarital affair, we look at five tech and startup leaders whose personal relationships or workplace controversies made headlines and, in some cases, led to resignations and dismissals.
item.content:encoded:
They built successful businesses, shaped industries and became some of the most influential names in technology. But for some, it was controversy over their personal lives, rather than competition or business failure, that disrupted their careers.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is the latest tech leader to face such scrutiny. His admission of an extramarital affair has come amid allegations of foreign intelligence activity, an independent board investigation and a shareholder lawsuit. Huang continues to lead Nvidia with the backing of its board, and the intelligence-related allegations remain contested.

On November 9, Nvidia and Huang were named in a proposed shareholder class-action lawsuit alleging that they misled investors by failing to disclose his reported relationship with a businesswoman suspected by US authorities of working for Chinese intelligence, Reuters reported. The lawsuit followed Nvidia's November 8 announcement of an investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or US national security have been compromised. China has rejected the espionage allegations.

Huang's controversy brings to mind five other cases involving prominent tech and startup executives in India and abroad, although the allegations and outcomes differ.

Phaneesh Murthy: The Indian IT executive dismissed by iGate

In May 2013, Phaneesh Murthy was dismissed as president and CEO of US-listed IT services company iGate following an investigation into his relationship with a subordinate employee. Murthy had earlier helped build Infosys' international business before leaving the company in 2002 following a sexual harassment lawsuit, which was subsequently settled out of court. He later founded Quintant Services, acquired by iGate, and went on to oversee iGate's expansion, including its $1.2 billion acquisition of Patni Computer Systems in 2011.

In a statement on May 20, 2013, iGate said an investigation by outside legal counsel had found that Murthy failed to disclose a relationship with a subordinate, violating company policy and his employment contract. The company said its investigation had not uncovered a violation of its sexual harassment policy at that stage. Murthy acknowledged the relationship but disputed the company's account of the disclosure and denied the harassment allegations. Following his dismissal, iGate shares fell approximately 13%, Reuters reported.

Murthy later founded IT advisory firm Primentor, where he has served as CEO. In June 2025, enterprise AI company Covasant announced his appointment as a strategic advisor to help expand its global business.

Arunabh Kumar: The TVF founder who stepped down but was later acquitted

In June 2017, Arunabh Kumar, founder of digital entertainment company The Viral Fever (TVF), stepped down as CEO after sexual harassment allegations surfaced against him. The allegations first appeared in an anonymous online account by a woman claiming to be a former TVF employee. Other women subsequently made similar allegations. Kumar denied wrongdoing. TVF's then Chief Operating Officer Dhawal Gusain took over as CEO, while Kumar continued as a mentor to the content team.

In September 2022, a Mumbai magistrate's court acquitted Kumar in a sexual harassment case registered against him in 2017. According to PTI, the court found that the prosecution had failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt, citing inconsistencies in the evidence and an unexplained delay in filing the complaint. The court also observed that the complaint could have arisen from a grudge or business rivalry.

Kumar remains associated with TVF. In January 2026, the company announced a leadership restructuring under which he would focus on mentoring producers and showrunners while remaining involved in select creative projects.

Brian Krzanich: The Intel CEO who resigned over a consensual relationship

Brian Krzanich resigned as Intel CEO in June 2018 after the chipmaker discovered that he had previously been involved in a consensual relationship with an employee. Krzanich had spent more than three decades at Intel, joining as an engineer in 1982 before becoming CEO in 2013. Intel said an investigation by internal and external counsel confirmed that the relationship violated its non-fraternisation policy, which applied to all managers.

The board accepted his resignation and appointed Chief Financial Officer Robert Swan as interim CEO. Intel described the relationship as consensual and did not publicly establish that it was extramarital. The company did not announce any finding of sexual harassment.

Krzanich returned to a top executive position in October 2024, when he became president and CEO of Cerence, a Nasdaq-listed company developing AI-powered technology for the automotive industry. He continues to lead the company.

Andy Rubin: The Android creator and Google's $90M controversy

Andy Rubin, widely credited with creating Android, left Google in 2014 after helping establish the mobile operating system as a global platform. His departure was initially presented as amicable. However, a 2018 New York Times investigation reported that Google had investigated a sexual misconduct complaint involving Rubin and a female employee with whom he had been having an extramarital relationship.

The newspaper reported that Google had found the employee's allegation credible and that Rubin had received a $90 million exit package. Rubin denied the sexual misconduct allegations and disputed reports that he had been forced to leave Google. The revelations prompted protests involving thousands of Google employees in 2018 over the company's handling of sexual misconduct complaints and accountability for senior executives.

After leaving Google, Rubin founded technology investment firm Playground Global and smartphone company Essential Products, which shut down in 2020. In November 2025, The Information reported that he had launched Genki Robotics, a Tokyo-based startup working on humanoid robots. Rubin confirmed his involvement in the venture but declined to share further details.

Mark Hurd: The HP CEO who resigned following a conduct investigation

Mark Hurd resigned as chairman and CEO of Hewlett-Packard in August 2010 following an investigation prompted by a sexual harassment complaint from a former company contractor. HP said the investigation found no violation of its sexual harassment policy but identified breaches of its business conduct standards. Contemporaneous reports said the investigation had uncovered inaccurate expense reports involving Hurd's interactions with the contractor, who subsequently stated that they had not had a sexual relationship.

Hurd's departure was therefore linked to findings concerning business conduct, not a substantiated sexual harassment allegation or a confirmed extramarital affair. He subsequently joined Oracle, becoming its co-CEO in 2014. Hurd died on October 18, 2019, aged 62, after taking medical leave the previous month.

What the reported cases don't tell us

These five cases attracted significant media attention. But there is no reliable public count of how many workplace relationship disputes or misconduct complaints involving senior executives are handled internally or never formally reported.

Aon's 2024 Voice of Women study, which surveyed nearly 24,000 professional women across more than 560 Indian companies, found that 6% had experienced sexual harassment at least once. Fewer than half of those affected formally reported the incident to their employer. The survey did not specifically examine misconduct involving CEOs or senior executives, and cannot establish how many such cases remain undisclosed.

The circumstances of the five executives differ. Some resigned after company investigations identified policy violations. Others stepped down amid allegations they denied, while Kumar was subsequently acquitted. In Huang's case, Nvidia's investigation is ongoing and the intelligence-related allegations remain contested. He continues to lead the company with the board's support.
